```{r, include = FALSE}
# The examples use dplyr, tidyr, lubridate and flextable, which are optional
# packages. Without them the code is shown but not run.
have_pkgs <- all(vapply(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "lubridate", "flextable"), requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2,
                      eval = have_pkgs,
                      dev = if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) "ragg_png" else "png")

```

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !have_pkgs}
cat("*The examples on this page need the dplyr, tidyr, lubridate and flextable packages, which are not all installed here, so their output is not shown.*\n")
```

phwstyle applies the Public Health Wales (PHW) house style, as used by its
Communicable Disease Surveillance Centre (CDSC), to R outputs. You write
your analysis as usual, then add one function to style it. It is not an
official PHW product.

## Quick start

Load phwstyle and call `use_phw_ggplot()` once. Every chart after that is
in the PHW style, with no extra code on each plot.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(phwstyle)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(lubridate)

use_phw_ggplot()
```

## A worked example: one line list, five outputs

A surveillance summary usually needs the same handful of outputs: an
epidemic curve, rates over time, an age and sex breakdown, a table of
characteristics and a table of rates. Starting from one line list and a
table of populations, each of these takes a few lines, and they come out in
one style. The data here are made up.

```{r}
set.seed(2025)
n <- 600
pick <- function(values, prob) sample(values, n, replace = TRUE, prob = prob)

cases <- tibble(
  age      = floor(rbeta(n, 0.7, 0.7) * 90),
  onset    = as.Date("2025-01-06") + round(rgamma(n, 5, 0.12)) + if_else(age >= 65, 14, 0),
  organism = pick(c("Type 1", "Type 2", "Type 3"), c(0.5, 0.35, 0.15)),
  sex      = pick(c("Female", "Male"), c(0.5, 0.5)),
  area     = pick(paste("Area", LETTERS[1:5]), c(0.3, 0.25, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1)),
  outcome  = pick(c("Outcome X", "Outcome Y"), c(0.85, 0.15))
) |>
  mutate(
    age_group = case_when(age < 15 ~ "0-14", age < 45 ~ "15-44", age < 65 ~ "45-64", TRUE ~ "65+"),
    age_band  = cut(age, c(seq(0, 80, 10), Inf), right = FALSE,
                    labels = c("0-9", "10-19", "20-29", "30-39", "40-49", "50-59", "60-69", "70-79", "80+"))
  )

population <- tibble(age_group  = c("0-14", "15-44", "45-64", "65+"),
                     population = c(52000, 118000, 81000, 64000))
```

### Three charts in one figure

`phw_epicurve()` and `phw_pyramid()` are ready-made public health charts.
The chart of weekly rates is ordinary dplyr and ggplot2, and
`phw_arrange()` puts the three together under one title and source line.

Each chart colours a different thing, so each has its own colours. The
organisms take the default palette. Age groups have an order, so they get
shades of one colour. In the pyramid the side already tells the sexes
apart, so two quiet colours are enough.

```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7.5, out.width = "100%", eval = have_pkgs && requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)}
curve <- phw_epicurve(cases, onset, group = organism) +
  labs(title = "Cases by week of onset", x = "Week beginning", y = "Cases")

weekly_rates <- cases |>
  count(week = floor_date(onset, "week", week_start = 1), age_group, name = "cases") |>
  complete(week, age_group, fill = list(cases = 0)) |>
  left_join(population, by = "age_group") |>
  mutate(rate = 100000 * cases / population)

rates_over_time <- ggplot(weekly_rates, aes(week, rate, colour = age_group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_phw_d(palette = tail(phw_palettes$greens, 4)) +
  labs(title = "Weekly rate per 100,000 by age group", x = "Week beginning", y = "Cases per 100,000")

pyramid <- phw_pyramid(cases, age_band, sex, percent = TRUE,
                       palette = phw_col("gold_465", "text_secondary")) +
  labs(title = "Cases by age and sex", x = "Percentage of cases")

figure <- phw_arrange(curve, rates_over_time, pyramid, design = "AA\nBC", guides = "keep",
                      title = "Summary of cases, January to May 2025",
                      source = "Example data", date = as.Date("2025-05-31"))
figure
```

When two charts show the same groups, give both the same colour key, for
example `scale_fill_phw_d(key = "organism")`, and each group keeps its
colour in every chart. See the
[Colours](`r site`articles/colours.html#colours-that-stay-with-their-groups)
article.

### A table of characteristics

`phw_summary_table()` counts each characteristic and works out the
percentages and the total column. `phw_flextable()` renders the result for
Word, PDF or HTML.

```{r}
characteristics <- cases |>
  phw_summary_table(vars = c(age_group, sex, area), by = outcome,
                    labels = list(age_group = "Age group", sex = "Sex", area = "Area",
                                  outcome = "Outcome"))

phw_flextable(characteristics, caption = "Characteristics of cases by outcome",
              source = "Example data")
```

### Rates with confidence intervals

`phw_rate_table()` takes counts and populations and returns rates per
100,000 with exact confidence intervals.

```{r}
rates <- cases |>
  count(age_group, name = "cases") |>
  left_join(population, by = "age_group") |>
  phw_rate_table(age_group, cases, population, labels = list(age_group = "Age group"))

phw_flextable(rates, caption = "Cases per 100,000 population by age group",
              source = "Example data")
```

Apart from the colours chosen for age group and sex in the figure, none of
this code sets a colour, a font, a border or a number format. Columns
are given as in dplyr: unquoted names, `c(a, b)` for several, or helpers
such as `starts_with()`. Strings work too.

### The same results in any output

The figure and the two tables are ordinary objects, so the same ones go
into a report, a workbook or a slide:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Excel: one sheet per table, with the same headings and number formats
phw_write_xlsx(list(Characteristics = characteristics, Rates = rates), "tables.xlsx")

# PowerPoint: one slide with the figure
phw_pptx() |>
  phw_add_slide("Summary of cases", plot = figure, source = "Example data") |>
  print(target = "summary.pptx")
```

For a whole report, name a phwstyle format in the YAML header of an R
Markdown document, and every chart and table in it is styled:

```yaml
output: phwstyle::phw_word_document
```

For Quarto, run `use_phw_quarto()` once in the project and use
`format: phw-docx` (or `phw-html`, `phw-typst` and others), then call
`use_phw_ggplot()` in the setup chunk.

## Which function do I need?

| I want to | Use | More in |
|---|---|---|
| Style every chart in a script | `use_phw_ggplot()` | [Charts](`r site`articles/charts.html) |
| Change the style of one chart | `theme_phw()`, `scale_fill_phw_d()` and the other PHW scales | [Charts](`r site`articles/charts.html) |
| Draw an epidemic curve, population pyramid, funnel plot or SPC chart | `phw_epicurve()`, `phw_pyramid()`, `phw_funnel()`, `phw_spc()` | [Charts](`r site`articles/charts.html#public-health-charts) |
| Put a second measure on its own axis | `phw_sec_axis()` | [Charts](`r site`articles/charts.html#a-second-measure-on-its-own-axis) |
| Keep each group the same colour in every chart | `scale_fill_phw_d(key = "name")`, `phw_colour_key()` | [Colours](`r site`articles/colours.html#colours-that-stay-with-their-groups) |
| Use colour-blind safe colours everywhere | `use_phw_ggplot(palette = "accessible")` | [Colours](`r site`articles/colours.html#colour-blind-safe-colours) |
| Make a table of counts, rates or characteristics from raw data | `phw_group_table()`, `phw_summary_table()`, `phw_crosstab()`, `phw_rate_table()`, `phw_risk_table()` | [Tables](`r site`articles/tables.html) |
| Render a table for Word or PDF | `phw_flextable()` | [Tables](`r site`articles/tables.html) |
| Make an interactive table or chart | `phw_reactable()`, `phw_datatable()`, `phw_plotly()` | [Exporting](`r site`articles/exporting.html#interactive-tables) |
| Draw a map of Welsh areas | `phw_boundaries()`, `theme_phw_map()`, `phw_leaflet()` | [Maps](`r site`articles/maps.html) |
| Write a whole report, slides or a dashboard | `phw_word_document()` and friends, `use_phw_quarto()` | [Documents](`r site`articles/documents.html) |
| Save a chart to send on its own | `phw_finalise()`, `phw_save()` | [Charts](`r site`articles/charts.html#finishing-and-saving) |
| Write tables to Excel, or slides to PowerPoint | `phw_write_xlsx()`, `phw_pptx()` | [Exporting](`r site`articles/exporting.html) |
| Check what is installed | `phw_setup_check()` | |

The [gallery](`r site`articles/gallery.html) shows every kind of output
with the functions behind it.

## How the pieces fit together

phwstyle works at three levels. Something set at a wider level is already
done for everything inside it, so you don't repeat it lower down.

**1. Once for a document, project or session.** Each of these is a switch
you set once.

| Set once | What it switches on | So don't also add |
|---|---|---|
| An R Markdown format: `phw_html_document()`, `phw_word_document()`, `phw_pdf_document()` | The page design (fonts, headings, header band, Word or LaTeX template, figure sizes), and it calls `use_phw_ggplot()` and `use_phw_flextable()` for you | `use_phw_ggplot()` or `use_phw_flextable()` in the document |
| A Quarto format: `phw-html`, `phw-docx`, `phw-typst` and the rest, after `use_phw_quarto()` | The page design only. A Quarto extension can't run R code, so call `use_phw_ggplot()` and `use_phw_flextable()` yourself in the setup chunk | |
| `use_phw_ggplot()` | For every ggplot: `theme_phw()`, the PHW palette for groups, PHW blues for numbers, navy for bars, lines and points that have no colour of their own, the PHW font in text layers, and the same for extension geoms | `+ theme_phw()` or `+ scale_*_phw_*()` on each plot, or `phw_style_extensions()` |
| `use_phw_flextable()` | PHW style for every flextable you make with flextable's own functions | `phw_flextable_theme()` on each table |
| `use_phw_gtsummary()` | PHW style for every gtsummary table. The document formats don't call this one, so add it when you use gtsummary | |
| The palette switch: `palette = "accessible"` in a format or in `use_phw_ggplot()`, or `options(phwstyle.palette = )` | Which colours groups get in every chart, table and widget | `palette = ` in each function |
| `options(phwstyle.font = )` | The font everywhere | |
| `phw_key_file()` | Where colour keys are kept between sessions. It colours nothing on its own: a key is used when you give a function `key = "name"` | |

**2. For one chart.** `theme_phw()` and `theme_phw_map()`, the colour and
fill scales (`scale_fill_phw_d()`, `scale_colour_phw_c()` and so on),
`scale_shape_phw()`, `scale_linetype_phw()` and `phw_sec_axis()` are added
to a plot with `+`, and affect only that plot.

**3. For one kind of chart or output.** The ready-made charts
(`phw_epicurve()`, `phw_pyramid()`, `phw_funnel()`, `phw_spc()`) bring
their own theme and colours, so they need no setup. So do the functions
that make a whole output: `phw_flextable()`, `phw_gt()`, `phw_reactable()`,
`phw_datatable()`, `phw_plotly()`, `phw_leaflet()`, `phw_write_xlsx()` and
`phw_add_slide()`. The setup functions at level 1 don't reach interactive
widgets, so use these each time (`phw_plotly(p)`, not
`plotly::ggplotly(p)`).
`phw_finalise()` and `phw_save()` are for a chart that leaves the report.

### Do I still need to add this?

"After setup" means inside a `phw_*_document()`, or after
`use_phw_ggplot()` in a script or Quarto document.

| You are about to add | Covered after setup? | Add it when |
|---|---|---|
| `+ theme_phw()` | Yes | You want different settings for this plot, e.g. `theme_phw(grid = "x")` or `legend = "right"` |
| `+ scale_fill_phw_d()` or `scale_colour_phw_d()` | Yes: groups get the PHW palette | You want a colour `key`, another `palette`, pinned `values`, a legend `name`, or "Other" and "Unknown" drawn in grey |
| `+ scale_fill_phw_c()` or `scale_colour_phw_c()` | Yes: numbers get PHW blues | You want another palette such as `"teals"`, or the full range including the palest blue |
| `fill = phw_col("navy")` inside a geom | Yes: bars, areas, lines and points are navy | You want a different colour |
| `family = phw_font()` in `geom_text()` | Yes | Never |
| `phw_style_extensions()` | Yes, for packages loaded before the setup ran | You load ggrepel, ggridges and the like afterwards |
| `scale_*_phw_b()` (binned) or `scale_*_phw_div()` (diverging) | No | The data need them, e.g. a choropleth in bands |
| `scale_shape_phw()`, `scale_linetype_phw()` | No | Groups should differ by more than colour |
| `theme_phw_map()` | No | The plot is a map |
| `labs(caption = phw_caption(...))` | No | The chart shows its source |
| `phw_finalise()` | No | The chart is used outside a branded report |

In a plain script with no setup, nothing is covered: add `+ theme_phw()`
and a PHW scale to each plot, or call `use_phw_ggplot()` at the top and
skip both. `use_phw_ggplot()` gives the same result on ggplot2 3.5 and
4.0. Without it, `+ theme_phw()` alone also gives groups the PHW palette
on ggplot2 4.0 (themes there can carry colours), but on ggplot2 3.5 it
styles only the text, gridlines and legend.

### Your changes win

Anything you add to a plot takes priority over the session and document
defaults. This is deliberate: the house style is a starting point, and you
can adjust on top of it when a chart needs something different.

* A scale added to a plot replaces the PHW default for that aesthetic. That
  goes for a PHW scale with other arguments, a ggplot2 scale such as
  `scale_fill_manual()`, and scales from other packages.
* `+ theme(...)`, or the same settings passed as arguments to
  `theme_phw(...)`, override the theme.
* `fill = ` or `colour = ` inside a geom overrides the default navy.
* A `palette = ` given to one function overrides the palette switch for
  that chart or table.

```{r}
ggplot(mpg, aes(class, fill = drv)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("4" = "#846AA4", f = "#338276", r = "#CFAB7A")) +
  theme(legend.position = "right") +
  labs(title = "A scale and a theme setting added to the plot replace the defaults",
       x = NULL, y = "Cars")
```

Two things follow from the same rule:

* `theme_phw()` is a complete theme, so adding it resets any `+ theme()`
  that came before it on that plot. Put your own `+ theme()` after it, or
  pass the settings to `theme_phw()`.
* The ready-made charts already have a fill or colour scale. Adding another
  one replaces theirs, and ggplot2 says so with "Scale for fill is already
  present". To change their colours, use their `palette` and `key`
  arguments instead.

## Colours

`phw_pal()` returns colours from the PHW palettes, and
`show_phw_palettes()` draws them all:

```{r}
phw_pal()                 # navy, teal, orange, pink: the default chart colours
phw_pal(6)                # more than four groups carry on into "extended"
phw_pal(5, "blues")       # sequential, for maps and heat tables
```

```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5}
show_phw_palettes()
```

Up to four groups use `main`. More carry on into `extended`, so a chart
with six groups starts with the same four colours as a chart with four.
`strategy` has the colours of the six priorities in the PHW Long-Term
Strategy, for work reported by priority; `blues`, `teals`, `greens` and
`gradient` are for numbers, and `orange_navy` for values either side of a
midpoint. Every `palette` argument also accepts your own vector of
colours.

### Colours that stay with their groups

If colours follow the order of the groups, adding a group (say a new age
band) shifts every colour after it. A colour key fixes each group's colour
instead. New groups get the next free colour, and existing ones never move.

```{r}
ages <- c("0-4", "5-14", "15-44", "45-64", "65+")
phw_colour_key(ages, "age_vignette")
phw_colour_key(c("Under 1", ages, "Unknown"), "age_vignette")
```

Use the key with `scale_colour_phw_d(key = "age_vignette")`, and the same
`key` in `phw_flextable_groups()`, `phw_reactable()` and
`phw_leaflet_polygons()`. To keep keys across sessions and reports, save
them to a file in your project with `phw_key_file("phw-colours.csv")`.

```{r, include = FALSE}
phw_key_reset("age_vignette")
```

### Colour-blind readers

The `accessible` palette stays distinct for all three common types of
colour blindness. It is not used unless you switch it on, and then every
chart, table and widget uses it, for any number of groups:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
use_phw_ggplot(palette = "accessible")  # or options(phwstyle.palette = "accessible")
```

In a document, add `phw-palette: accessible` to the YAML header, or set the
palette when you render to make a default and an accessible version of the
same document (see `?phw_default_palette`, and the
[Reports and documents](`r site`articles/documents.html#default-and-accessible-colours)
guide).

`accessible = TRUE` in `use_phw_ggplot()` or `theme_phw()` is a different
setting: it makes text larger and lines thicker, and leaves colours alone.

Colour should never be the only cue: add `scale_shape_phw()` or
`scale_linetype_phw()` to charts. To check any set of colours, and see them
as a colour-blind reader would:

```{r}
phw_check_colours("main")
```

```{r, fig.height = 3}
show_phw_palettes(c("main", "accessible", "rag", "rag_accessible"), cvd = "deutan")
```

The [Colours and accessibility](`r site`articles/colours.html) guide covers
all of this in more detail.

## Charts

Add `phw_caption()` as the caption to show the source line the way PHW
reports do. Use `theme_phw(grid = "x")` for horizontal bars and
`theme_phw_map()` for maps.

```{r}
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = drv, shape = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~year) +
  scale_shape_phw() +
  labs(title = "Engine size and fuel economy",
       x = "Engine size (litres)", y = "Miles per gallon",
       caption = phw_caption("ggplot2::mpg"))
```

The ready-made public health charts return ordinary ggplots, so you can
add titles and layers as usual:

```{r}
units <- tibble(unit = paste("Unit", 1:30), eligible = round(runif(30, 300, 6000))) |>
  mutate(events = rbinom(n(), eligible, c(rep(0.72, 28), 0.6, 0.82)))

phw_funnel(units, events, eligible, label = unit) +
  labs(title = "Proportion by unit", x = "Eligible population", y = "Proportion (%)")
```

Charts from ggplot2 extensions (ggalluvial, ggsankey, ggridges, ggrepel,
treemapify, ggtext and others) take the PHW scales like any other chart,
and `use_phw_ggplot()` restyles their own defaults. Load those packages
before calling it. `phw_arrange()` puts several charts in one figure with
one title and source line. `phw_finalise()` adds the logo and source
footer to a chart that will be shared on its own, and `phw_save()` saves it
at report size.

## Tables

Five builders make the tables PHW reports use most. Each returns a data
frame that renders with `phw_flextable()` (Word, PDF, HTML), `phw_gt()`,
`phw_reactable()` (interactive) and `phw_write_xlsx()` (Excel):

- `phw_summary_table()`: characteristics (age group, sex, risk factors...)
  as n (%) or median (IQR), optionally split by a group with a total column.
- `phw_crosstab()`: counts by two variables, with totals and row or column
  percentages.
- `phw_rate_table()`: rates per 100,000 with exact Poisson confidence
  intervals, for several demographic or risk variables at once.
- `phw_risk_table()`: attack rates and relative risks by exposure, as used
  in outbreak investigations.
- `phw_group_table()`: counts (or any statistic) with nested row and column
  groups, group totals and a table total.

```{r}
cases |>
  phw_group_table(rows = c(area, organism), cols = sex,
                  labels = list(area = "Area", organism = "Organism", sex = "Sex")) |>
  phw_flextable(caption = "Cases by area, organism and sex", source = "Example data")
```

For extra column formats, use `phw_flextable_heat()` and
`phw_flextable_bars()` in flextable, and `phw_col_bar()`, `phw_col_heat()`,
`phw_col_rag()` and `phw_col_percent()` in reactable.

## Maps

`phw_boundaries()` downloads boundaries for any level of Welsh geography and
keeps a copy in your cache folder, so later calls work offline.
`phw_boundary_levels()` lists the levels: country, health boards, local
authorities, GP clusters, Senedd and UK Parliament constituencies, electoral
wards, communities, middle and lower layer super output areas (MSOAs and
LSOAs), output areas, and fire and police areas.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
hb <- phw_boundaries("health_board")
ggplot(hb) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = name), colour = "white") +
  theme_phw_map() +
  labs(caption = attr(hb, "attribution"))
```

Join your data on the `code` column, which holds the official area codes
from the Office for National Statistics (ONS), such as W11000028, or on
`name`.

## More outputs

- gt and gtsummary: `phw_gt()` renders any data frame or summary table, and
  `use_phw_gtsummary()` styles every gtsummary table.
- Interactive: `phw_reactable()` and `phw_datatable()` for tables,
  `phw_plotly()` for any plotly chart or ggplot, and `phw_leaflet()` with
  `phw_leaflet_polygons()` for maps.
- Exports: `phw_write_xlsx()` for Excel, and `phw_pptx()` with
  `phw_add_slide()` for PowerPoint.
- Shiny: `phw_page_navbar()`, or `theme = phw_bs_theme()` in any bslib or
  Shiny page.

## Wording

Every label phwstyle writes can be changed. For example:

```{r}
phw_caption("Example data", date = as.Date("2026-11-03"))
phw_caption("Example data", source_prefix = "Data: ", note = "Provisional figures")
```

## Changing anything else

Most functions pass extra arguments to the function they wrap (the `...`
on each help page), so you can override a default: `theme_phw(plot.title = element_text(size = 18))`,
`phw_reactable(data, pagination = FALSE)`, `phw_plotly(p, hovermode = "x")`,
`phw_bs_theme(primary = "#24A2B5")`.

## Logos

The PHW logo is a trade mark and is not included in the package.
`phw_logo()` finds it in your `phwstyle.logo_dir` folder, or in a copy
saved by `phw_download_logos()`. Without a logo, outputs are still styled,
and show the organisation name instead.
